title: Atoms, isotopes and the mole
note: An atom's identity is set by its proton count, the atomic number Z. The mass number A counts protons plus neutrons, so isotopes of one element differ only in neutrons. The mole links atoms to grams: one mole is 6.022 × 10²³ particles, and an element's molar mass in g/mol equals its average atomic mass in u.

read.title: Counting atoms by weighing them
text: Atoms are far too small to count one by one, so chemists count them by mass. The tool that makes this possible is the mole. One mole is exactly 6.02214076 × 10²³ particles, a number chosen so that the mass of one mole in grams matches, for all practical purposes, the mass of one particle in atomic mass units.

The atomic mass unit is defined as one twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom. A single carbon-12 atom has a mass of exactly 12 u, so a mole of carbon-12 atoms has a mass of 12 grams. The atomic masses on the periodic table are weighted averages over each element's natural isotopes. Chlorine, for example, is a mix of chlorine-35 and chlorine-37, and its listed mass of about 35.45 u matches no single atom.

To find the molar mass of a compound, add the molar masses of its atoms. Water, H₂O, is about 2(1.008) + 16.00 = 18.02 g/mol. With that number you can move between grams and moles: 9.01 g of water is half a mole, which contains about 3.01 × 10²³ water molecules. Grams, moles, and particles are three views of the same amount of matter.

q.q: Why does chlorine's atomic mass of about 35.45 u match no single chlorine atom?
o: Chlorine atoms lose mass when they bond
It includes the mass of electrons twice
It is an average over chlorine's isotopes
